title: Conjuring: Leaking Control Flow via Speculative Fetch Attacks
problem: Modern CPUs leak control flow information through the Pattern History Table (PHT) during speculative instruction fetch. The attack can reconstruct victim application control flow without requiring explicit priming or victim process interference.
motivation: Speculative execution side-channels pose a fundamental security threat to confidentiality of applications running on contemporary processors across multiple vendors.
method: CPUs use a Pattern History Table (PHT—a hardware memory recording branch predictions to guess what instructions to fetch). When the CPU speculatively guesses which way a branch (decision point in code) will go, it updates the PHT; Conjuring observes these updates to figure out what control flow path the victim program actually took. Because this happens naturally during normal execution, no special setup or interference with the victim is needed. Improved branch predictor designs actually amplify this leak.
key_novelty: First practical side-channel attack that extracts victim control flow through the Pattern History Table without any special setup or victim interference, executable with unprivileged code.
contributions: Proposes Conjuring attack exploiting speculative fetch through Pattern History Table as a control flow channel
Demonstrates realistic threat model requiring no victim process cooperation or explicit cache priming
Validates attack effectiveness across Intel, AMD, and Apple CPU architectures
Shows that enhanced branch predictors increase attack practicality and information leakage

metrics.other: control flow information leakage per branch query, attack success rate

primary_theme: Speculative execution side-channel via branch predictor
